correctness.rationale: Binomidness forces f2/f1 and f3/f1 integral. For ordered nonnegative root shifts, u_t=(t+2)/(t+1) is decreasing: a>=3 is impossible, and b is bounded by 3,5,3 for a=0,1,2. Solving c+1=K/(m-K) for exact integer m yields exactly twelve triples, displayed with their f3/f1 fractions; nine fail the second test. The three survivors equal n^3, 2n*C2(n), and 6*C3(n), all binomid by the ordinary binomial theorem, product closure, and the published integer binomial-determinant identity. The included pure-Python exact verifier confirms twelve candidates, 15,450 sample coefficients and 350 determinant cases. Computation does not replace the unrestricted proof; no claim about cubics outside the specified root class is made.

originality.rationale: Relative to the inspected full primary materials, Shapiro establishes degree-at-most-two classification and states the cubic case as Open Problem 27. Its known Pascal-column examples and product closure establish positive cases, not exhaustive exclusions. Caalim–Tanaka give general binomid-index machinery but no integer-root cubic finite recognition theorem. Targeted equivalence, parameter, table and broader-coverage searches found no dominating classification. Residual uncertainty concerning unindexed equivalent work remains explicit.
residual_risks: An equivalent proof of this integer-root cubic subclass might exist in unindexed mathematical literature or later work not recovered by the searches.

value.rationale: The published cubic-polynomial classification problem naturally separates by root geometry. All cubics with three nonpositive integer roots form an unbounded, three-parameter subclass. The result gives a complete classification of this subclass and an exact constant-size recognition certificate from its first three values, despite infinitely many generalized-binomial integrality requirements. It excludes every other root-shift triple uniformly rather than relying on a finite census. This is a motivated natural classification, not an arbitrary parameter slice or a rebranding of a known positive example. No downstream general theorem is asserted.
